Relative to the no-reference path, the tracking score is higher by 0.306 and 0.415 without news and by 0.183 and 0.329 with news; within the stock/cash scan structural bias is lowest at 70/30 (B=0.042); realization peaks at a 3:7 technical share (R=0.894 versus 0.358 for technical-only); and Delta is 0.0341 with fundamental data and 0.0487 with news. Both stages use the same two observable scores, each read in the regime where it is interpretable.

title: SAR-TopoGuard: Training-Free, Speckle-Aware Topological Verification for Structure-Preserving SAR-to-Optical Translation
justification: Training-free inference-time verification layer for SAR-to-optical translation; vision not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Remote-sensing niche despite inference-time framing.
abstract: SAR-to-optical translators often synthesize detail that the radar measurement does not support, and pixel metrics alone cannot reveal it. We propose SAR-TopoGuard, a training-free inference-time layer for frozen generators: a stochastic sampler draws K candidates (Monte Carlo dropout for GANs, seed variance for diffusion), a speckle-aware verifier ranks them by gradient-magnitude correlation with the SAR input and a hallucination-frequency index, and a SAR-guided frequency gate admits high-frequency detail only where SAR edges support it. With all five hyperparameters frozen and three training seeds, we evaluate on 500 scene-disjoint SEN1-2 test patches, 500 patches of a held-out summer scene, and 200 cross-dataset SEN12MS winter pairs. The layer improves Pix2Pix by +0.060, +0.012, and +0.077 dB PSNR and by +0.0034, +0.0057, and +0.0135 SSIM, respectively (Wilcoxon p < 1e-6), and it improves CycleGAN and CUT on all three sets (+0.013 to +0.076 dB). It raises edge precision at the cost of edge recall (edge F1 -1.3% on the test set). On the latent diffusion model COP-GEN, it adds +0.33 dB (base) and +0.16 dB (Beta) on the winter set, the only set with dual-polarization SAR. An ablation shows that the gate produces the gain for MC-dropout GANs, whose candidates are nearly identical, whereas verifier selection contributes up to +0.26 dB for diffusion, whose samples differ. The layer has zero trainable parameters and adds 0.4 ms per patch beyond the K=5 generator passes.

title: Hardening Agentic Web Populations Through Multi-Criterion Competitive Co-Evolution: Lessons from Wargame Strategy Optimization
justification: Co-evolution framing for agent jailbreak/guardrails; position paper not inference.
hype_justification: Safety arms-race framing, moderate discussion appeal.
abstract: Agents on the open web will face adversaries that keep adapting, so a defense that is only tested once will eventually be found and broken. We propose treating jailbreak attacks and safety guardrails as two populations that evolve against each other, rather than as a fixed attacker probing a fixed defense. This idea comes directly from wargame strategy optimization, where two-population competitive co-evolution with alternating evolution cycles and cross-play evaluation has already been shown to produce strategies that are robust to a moving opponent, and where a companion line of work has shown that the same machinery can measure how much competitive pressure a population must absorb. However, real-world applications can never rely on a single criterion as a key performance indicator, rather must use multiple conflicting criteria, such as, cost and efficiency. We describe how this mechanism transfers to language model safety, argue why the resulting multi-criteria, competitive and coevolutionary arms race is a genuinely networked, population-level problem rather than a two-agent toy setting, and lay out the open problems that stand between the wargame version of this idea and an agentic web version of it.

title: From Mutation to Medication: Characterizing Failures of Clinical LLMs to Respect Genomic Resistance
justification: Failures of clinical LLMs on genomic resistance; evaluation not inference.
hype_justification: Clinical-safety failure analysis across many models draws some attention.
abstract: Language models are increasingly proposed to support molecular tumour boards, but may recommend cancer therapies despite genomic evidence of resistance. We evaluated ten models on 1,464 resistance cases from five curated oncology knowledge bases, collecting 58,910 judgments. Models endorsed resisted therapies in 21.8-81.4% of cases. However, raw rates can reflect a tendency to agree rather than an ability to distinguish resistance from drug sensitivity: one open-weight model endorsed 81.4% of resistance cases and 82.3% of sensitivity controls. We therefore compared endorsement within matched gene and evidence-level groups. This analysis is exploratory because it was specified after the pre-registered analysis, which yielded null-to-weak results. Measured failures depended strongly on the reference knowledge base and evidence strength. When a second source independently confirmed resistance, four models across three vendors endorsed at most 2.4% of cases; at weaker evidence tiers, discrimination was not measurable. Models sometimes acknowledged resistance yet recommended the therapy. Repeating a model's own resistance conclusion reduced endorsement to 0.0-3.5% on cases where it had stated resistance. Falsely attributing the opposite conclusion increased endorsement above baseline for all seven hosted models, reaching 95.2% for GPT-4o; an instruction without an attributed conclusion changed endorsement by only 0.9 percentage points. Providing the correct curated evidence reduced unqualified strong recommendations to 0.3-3.5%, testing evidence use under an oracle condition rather than retrieval.

title: OmitEHR: Scalable Omission Detection in LLM-Generated Clinical Summaries
justification: Omission detection in LLM clinical summaries; application not inference systems.
hype_justification: Practical clinical tooling with efficiency gains, domain interest.
abstract: Health systems increasingly rely on large language models (LLMs) to draft summaries of patient medical records, yet evaluations now find omissions, the absence of clinically important information, to be the most common failure mode. Detecting omissions in an LLM-generated summary requires knowing which facts in the record are salient, a signal that existing methods hand-specify, ignore, or recompute at inference with costly LLM judges. We present OmitEHR, a reference-free omission detector that learns clinical salience from historical clinician-written summaries predating widespread LLM use. OmitEHR learns to predict which source-note sentences clinicians include in their summaries, then surfaces high-salience sentences not covered by an LLM-generated summary as candidate omissions. We apply OmitEHR to brief hospital course (BHC) summarization using 5,000 admissions from a large academic medical center. On held-out admissions, OmitEHR outperformed all evaluated baselines at predicting salient source sentences, including a prompted LLM judge. The full omission detection pipeline took 17.7 to 19.5 seconds and cost \$0.03 to \$0.13 per summary depending on the base model, 1.6 to 1.7 times faster and 5.6 to 6.7 times cheaper than scoring every source sentence with an LLM judge. In a blinded review of 25 admissions, two board-certified clinicians confirmed a mean of 5.6 clinically meaningful omissions per summary surfaced by OmitEHR, compared with 3.3 for a full LLM pipeline, counting candidates confirmed by at least one clinician. The efficiency and validity of OmitEHR make it a practical tool for health systems to flag omissions before a summary reaches the clinician.

title: Delay-Aware Reinforcement Learning for O-RAN Control under Stochastic Reward Feedback
justification: Delay-aware RL for O-RAN control; telecom RL not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Specialized O-RAN venue.
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is increasingly employed for real-time control in Open Radio Access Networks (O-RANs). However, the asynchronous nature of O-RAN feedback introduces stochastic delays between actions and their observable rewards, leading to misaligned credit assignment and unstable training. This letter formulates the O-RAN control problem as a Markov decision process (MDP) with delayed and stochastic rewards, where the true reward corresponding to an action is received after an unknown delay. To address this, we propose a delay-aware deep RL framework that integrates a long short-term memory (LSTM)-based delay predictor and a temporal reward realignment module within an off-policy learning pipeline. Using empirical delay traces collected from the Open AI Cellular (OAIC) testbed, we demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves faster convergence and significantly reduces latency violations and packet drops compared to conventional RL methods that ignore feedback delay. The results confirm that reward-delay compensation is critical for reliable AI-driven O-RAN control.

title: Information Limits of Replay-Free Recurrent State Migration
justification: Information limits of replay-free recurrent state migration; recurrent-model state theory, tangential to KV/cache.
hype_justification: Theoretical, niche audience despite recurrent-model relevance.
abstract: When a recurrent model is replaced, its old state may not determine what the new model would compute from the same history. We characterize the information that must be retained before the replacement is known. For a time-invariant affine linear family, the minimum continuous causal memory for order-$k$ local migration equals the reachable dimension of a lifted coefficient system minus the information in the anchor state. A controllable $d$-state model with scalar input needs at most $kd$ additional real coordinates, even when arbitrary matrix replacement directions are revealed only after streaming. A single rank-one direction can already require all $kd$. Conditional singular values and auxiliary-bit bounds distinguish this local information law from recovery at a fixed tolerance. We also give invariant-subspace and future-output constructions. Controlled experiments compare the resulting representations. In a small language model, equal-memory cubic interpolation improves mean state fidelity over third-order coefficients but provides no meaningful predictive gain. An analytic history basis preserves useful adaptation more economically in a coupled identification task. With repeated slow poles, eight history coordinates meet normalized output error $10^{-4}$ across five fitted seeds despite substantial full-state error. Splitting the poles raises the smallest tested successful width to 64.

title: SMELL: Sparsity-aware Memory Efficient Federated Fine-tuning for Long-context LLMs
justification: Sparsity-aware memory-efficient federated fine-tuning for long-context LLMs; memory/efficiency but training-side.
hype_justification: Long-context + memory efficiency is of interest; federated niche.
abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables Large Language Models (LLMs) to collaboratively adapt to distributed private data. However, long-context fine-tuning on resource-constrained devices faces substantial challenges arising from excessive activation memory, heterogeneous token-importance patterns across clients, and communication overhead. To address these challenges, we propose SMELL, a Sparsity-aware and Memory-Efficient federated fine-tuning framework for Long-context LLMs. SMELL integrates three complementary mechanisms: Local Sparse-Forward Adaptation (LSFA), Consensus-Anchored Sparsity Coordination (CASC), and Communication-Efficient Progressive Update Recovery (CPUR). These mechanisms jointly enable memory-efficient local adaptation, heterogeneity-aware sparsity coordination, and lightweight model-update transmission. Experiments on OPT-350M and LLaMA2-7B demonstrate that SMELL reduces peak memory consumption by up to 88.35% compared with conventional fine-tuning and 13.25% compared with forward-only LoRA fine-tuning at a 16K context length. Furthermore, SMELL improves fine-tuning performance under certain non-IID settings and supports compact update transmission with progressive reconstruction, demonstrating its potential for resource-efficient federated long-context LLM adaptation.

title: A Comparative Evaluation of BERT-Based and LLM-Based Models for Indic Sentence Similarity
justification: BERT vs LLM embeddings for Indic sentence similarity; evaluation not inference.
hype_justification: Multilingual embedding comparison, narrow audience.
abstract: The relative effectiveness of BERT-based encoders and large language model (LLM)-based embeddings for Indic semantic textual similarity remains insufficiently characterized. We compare eight BERT-based and five LLM-based models on the 1,500-pair STS Benchmark development set translated into ten Indic languages and on the native Marathi MahaSTS test set. IndicSBERT achieves the highest Pearson correlation in all ten translated language sets, with a macro-average of 0.843, followed by BGE-M3 at 0.792. Harrier-270M is the strongest LLM-based model on translated STS-B, with a macro-average of 0.751. On MahaSTS, IndicSBERT and Bhasha-Embed-v0 achieve Pearson correlations of 0.901 and 0.900, respectively, while EmbeddingGemma leads the LLM-based models at 0.871. The highest-scoring BERT-based model thus exceeds the highest-scoring LLM-based model in both settings, although the magnitude of the difference varies across benchmarks. These findings indicate that LLM-derived embeddings do not uniformly improve Indic sentence similarity over established encoders and motivate evaluation that accounts for language coverage, task supervision, and benchmark construction.

title: Enforcing Ellipsoidal Constraints in Neural Networks with a Polynomial Safety Layer
justification: Polynomial safety layer for ellipsoidal NN constraints; control not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Control/robotics-safety niche.
abstract: Often the output of a learned mapping must satisfy prescribed constraints. In the control of autonomous systems, for example, the chosen action must keep the system within a collision-free region. We consider the case in which a proposed output is corrected by projection onto a safety ellipsoid. Computing this projection amounts to solving a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP). We construct a neural-network safety layer by unrolling a feasibility-preserving polynomial penalty iteration. The unrolled structure allows the loss gradient to propagate from the feasible output through the safety layer to the network parameters during training. We show how to choose the layer parameters so that every iterate is feasible and give a computable bound on its distance to the exact projection at any prescribed depth. We illustrate the method by training a LiDAR-based policy to control an unmanned aerial vehicle. A privileged model predictive control expert uses the map and the measured vehicle state to generate the training data. In the simulated narrow mazes, the filtered policy avoided wall contact at every tested stage of training, including at initialization, when every unfiltered flight hit a wall. A representative build of the learned policy and its safety layer for an Arm Cortex-M4F microcontroller occupies about 36 KiB of flash, with a RAM budget below 5 KiB.

title: CausalGloss: Multi-Evidence Action Control for a Simultaneous Mandarin Speech-to-ASL Gloss Cascade
justification: Simultaneous speech-to-ASL gloss cascade; translation not inference systems.
hype_justification: Sign-language translation niche.
abstract: Simultaneous Mandarin speech-to-American Sign Language (ASL) gloss translation requires deciding when an evolving utterance supports committing each gloss. Fixed Wait-k cannot adapt to source-gloss reordering, while training only on reference histories causes exposure bias. We present CausalGloss, an English-prefix-to-ASL-gloss action policy for a Mandarin-speech cascade. It combines lexical and semantic evidence, bounded delay, negation constraints, burst WRITE actions, and incomplete-history recovery. On a frozen 500-example How2Sign-derived benchmark with weak LLM-generated references, CausalGloss improves the fixed Wait-k frontier and nearly matches a three-seed TransLLaMA-style learned adaptive baseline at k = 5 in Token F1 (0.7047 versus 0.7067), with 54.4% lower LAAL. Against CLERC Epee human-gloss references, it achieves 0.649 Token F1 and Pareto-dominates three-seed TransLLaMA-style k = 5 and fixed k = 5, 7, reducing LAAL by 58.2-69.9%. Ablations separate timing from retention. A synthetic Mandarin-speech cascade preserves a smaller computation-aware latency gain, although outputs remain over-long. We also construct ChineseSpeech-ASLGloss-v1, a 19,924-utterance, 36.54-h controlled evaluation corpus.

title: Does a completed simulation run mean a usable urban wind result for AI agents?
justification: Agents running urban-wind CFD; scientific-agent application not inference.
hype_justification: CFD-agent benchmark, narrow engineering audience.
abstract: AI agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now configure and run computational fluid dynamics (CFD) solvers, but a completed run does not ensure that delivered metrics can be recomputed from raw outputs. This gap was examined for urban wind simulation, where multi-case comparisons must hold non-target conditions fixed and reported values must be traceable to raw samples. UrbanWind-AgentBench, comprising 200 tasks and 367 cases in 10 engineering task families, was constructed. Public task contracts specify variable factors, fixed conditions, numerical thresholds and deliverable requirements, and two-layer scoring separates a structural score for deliverables, run provenance and raw evidence from a numerical score obtained by independent recomputation against references. WindPilot was then proposed as an execution framework that incorporates contract parsing, execution provenance, deterministic verification and bounded acceptance review into the LLM execution loop. On 30 OpenFOAM tasks with independent references, at least the structural maximum of 60 points was reached by a base agent on 28 tasks, but numerical credit was obtained on only 6. With the same model name and budget, WindPilot increased the number of tasks with numerical credit to 17, full-score tasks from 0 to 3 and the mean task score from 62.5 to 72.5. Mean action steps fell from 130.4 to 104.9, and mean token consumption decreased by 12.9%. The mean gain for atmospheric boundary layer (ABL) tasks was 18.5 points. A completed simulation run is therefore not sufficient for a usable urban wind result; usability depends on checks that tie reported metrics to raw evidence during execution.

title: SARGO: Agreement-Gated Reinforcement and Suppression via On-Policy Self-Guidance for Visual Hallucination Mitigation
justification: RL for visual hallucination mitigation in VLMs; training not inference serving.
hype_justification: Hallucination mitigation is popular, incremental RL method.
abstract: Vision-language models remain susceptible to visual hallucinations, often mixing grounded information with unsupported claims in the same response. Response-level reinforcement learning assigns a shared advantage to all tokens in a response, causing negative updates to suppress correct information alongside unsupported claims. To reduce hallucination while preserving useful visual information, we introduce SARGO (Self-guided Advantage-Routed Grounding Optimization), a post-training framework for selective reinforcement and suppression through on-policy self-guidance. Direct and reciprocal weighting gives better-supported tokens stronger reinforcement on positive updates and weaker penalties on negative updates. Agreement between overall and hallucination-specific advantages selects when to apply this guidance. At the response level, a reference-calibrated reward couples factuality with the retention and expansion of grounded information, discouraging lower hallucination scores obtained through omission. Experiments on Qwen3-VL-4B, Qwen3-VL-8B, and Gemma3-4B demonstrate that SARGO outperforms the evaluated mitigation baselines across Obj-Hal, AMBER, THRONE, and SHR evaluations. SARGO achieves these gains while preserving useful visual information and general multimodal capabilities.

title: Pixel-KWS: Rendered-Glyph Representations for Orthographically Robust Open-Vocabulary Keyword Spotting
justification: Rendered-glyph keyword spotting; speech/robustness not LLM inference.
hype_justification: KWS niche.
abstract: Open-vocabulary keyword spotting (KWS) allows users to enroll arbitrary keywords at inference time. However, character and phoneme-based text encoders rely on fixed symbol vocabularies learned during training, limiting their ability to handle unseen or visually similar symbols such as homoglyphs, l33tspeak substitutions, and accented characters. We propose PIXEL-KWS, an open-vocabulary KWS framework that represents characters through rendered glyphs rather than learned embedding lookups. We render each character as a grayscale image and encode it with a lightweight CNN, enabling the text encoder to generalize from visual form rather than a fixed vocabulary. On LibriPhrase, PIXEL-KWS and its matched character-based counterpart achieve 9.57% and 9.55% EER on LibriPhrase-hard, 0.43% and 0.41% EER on LibriPhrase-easy, outperforming all published baselines without pre-training or synthetic data. PIXEL-KWS provides substantially greater robustness to both homoglyph and l33tspeak symbol-level perturbations. These results highlight glyph-based representations as a simple and effective approach for robust open-vocabulary KWS in practical settings.

title: From Facts to Personas: Interpretable Role Unlearning in LLMs via Mixture-of-Experts
justification: MoE-based role unlearning for persona forgetting; unlearning not inference serving.
hype_justification: Unlearning + MoE interpretability, moderate interest with code release.
abstract: LLMs are widely adopted in multi-role dialogue and persona simulation. However, their strong ability to imitate role-specific linguistic and behavioral patterns can introduce privacy risks, reinforce social biases, and lead to unsafe or uncontrollable outputs. To address these issues, we introduce the Role-playing Unlearning task, which aims to selectively forget the style and knowledge associated with target roles while preserving the language ability and behaviors of the remaining roles. Unlike prior unlearning tasks that focus solely on removing factual information, our task additionally requires forgetting persona-specific characteristics, making the control over model generation more fine-grained. We propose RoleMoE, a Mixture-of-Experts framework that maps different roles to more independent expert subspaces, improving role separation and structural interpretability. To further distinguish role-specific features, RoleMoE incorporates two complementary losses: a specialization loss that drives roles to adopt distinct expert distributions, and a disentanglement loss that encourages experts to develop distinct capability subspaces. This decomposed structure enables role unlearning to focus selectively on target-role experts. We finally propose RoleBench-Unlearn for evaluation, and experiments on multiple backbone LLMs show that RoleMoE enables precise and controllable role forgetting, while better preserving the linguistic quality, knowledge, and persona consistency of non-target roles. All code and datasets are publicly available at: https://github.com/mbzuai-nlp/ROLEMOE.

title: Confidence Without Cause: Predicting and Localizing Physics-Shortcut Sensitivity in Language Model Hidden States
justification: Predicting physics-shortcut sensitivity in hidden states; interpretability not inference.
hype_justification: Hidden-state monitoring niche.
abstract: A language model's confidence on a physics problem deserves trust only if it ignores details irrelevant to the answer. We introduce DECOY (Distractor-Embedded Certified cOunterfactuals for phYsics): 155 families of four prompts differing in one irrelevant detail. A symbolic solver certifies that each edit preserves the answer. Families are labelled by the largest drop in the model's log-probability of the certified answer, using a threshold fixed before probe training. Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is sensitive on 50.0% of the 140 families yielding labels, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on 22.9%. Effects are largest when distractor values lie numerically close to the answer. A linear probe on Qwen's layer-18 hidden state, averaged over four renderings, predicts sensitivity before generation at AUROC 0.760 with whole families held out. A separately tuned single-rendering probe reaches 0.747. A frozen layer-16 probe reaches 0.820 pooled AUROC on 15 families built after training, though within-cue-type AUROC is lower (0.667-0.6875). Under a paired family bootstrap, the probe performs on par with a fitted token-entropy baseline (AUROC 0.727) and achieves the lowest Brier score among tested predictors (0.204 versus 0.214). Knocking out four attention heads at layer 16 cancels sensitivity on a 20-family panel, localising it to a narrow mechanism. These results show that Qwen's confidence can track irrelevant details, that this failure is detectable before generation, and that targeted intervention can suppress it. DECOY provides certified ground truth and paired-tested baselines for evaluating hidden-state monitors.

title: PMR: MoE Routing with Shared Prototypes and Congestion Pricing
justification: Prototype-mediated MoE routing with congestion pricing and load balancing; relevant to MoE serving efficiency though training-focused.
hype_justification: MoE routing/load balancing is a hot area; solid pretraining results.
abstract: Conventional linear routers in sparse mixture-of-experts models select experts directly from token-expert matching scores, coupling input matching with expert allocation. We propose Prototype-Mediated Routing (PMR), a two-stage router with shared prototypes. PMR first computes each token's distribution over prototypes, then uses it to mix prototype-conditioned expert distributions according to the law of total probability. This formulation models input matching and expert allocation separately, explicitly represents many-to-many associations between prototypes and experts, and provides separate interfaces for context adaptation and load regulation. Within this framework, short-term states summarize preceding tokens to adapt the prototypes, while congestion prices updated from dispatch feedback achieve loss-free load balancing by adjusting the conditional expert distributions. We use a two-pass blockwise approximation to accelerate short-term state processing, achieving over 20 times the training throughput of the eager tokenwise PMR implementation while maintaining high agreement in routing decisions. Across three pretraining configurations with 0.43B, 1.18B, and 0.48B total parameters, PMR improves mean zero-shot accuracy on seven benchmarks over linear routing baselines with matched expert architectures by 1.54, 2.65, and 1.45 percentage points (pp), respectively. The corresponding gains on ARC-Easy are 6.71, 5.80, and 3.92 pp. In parameter-efficient fine-tuning of 7B-8B backbones, PMR's improvements over MixLoRA vary across backbones, with gains of up to 1.76 pp in mean accuracy across four tasks.

title: Real-World End-to-End Product Entity Resolution
justification: Product entity resolution pipelines; application not inference systems.
hype_justification: E-commerce ER niche.
abstract: Product Entity Resolution (PER) in e-commerce is challenging due to unstructured text, formatting inconsistencies, promotional noise, and fine-grained product differences. We present an end-to-end evaluation of four zero-shot PER pipelines---Lexical Cascade, Semantic Cascade, Hybrid Fusion Cascade, and Generative-Lexical Cascade---across established benchmarks and introduce two real-world datasets characterized by cross-lingual noise and dense brand collisions. We evaluate lexical and dense blocking with cross-encoder, tensor-search, and Large Language Model verification, considering accuracy, runtime, and memory consumption.

title: Do Rule-Based Tools Help LLMs Translate Endangered Uralic Languages in the Prompt or over MCP?
justification: Rule-based tools for endangered-language translation via MCP; translation study not inference.
hype_justification: Low-resource translation + MCP, modest interest.
abstract: Komi-Zyrian, Moksha, Erzya and Udmurt have mature rule-based resources, among them finite-state analysers, constraint grammars and bilingual dictionaries, which language models do not use. We ask whether giving a model access to these resources improves machine translation from the four languages into English, and whether it matters how the access is provided: as analyses computed in advance and written into the prompt, or as tools that the model calls itself through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). We evaluate manually: an expert linguist read every English output of the strongest model under three conditions, 816 sentences in all, accepted or rejected each one, and named the main error in every rejected translation. With the analyses in the prompt, the number of accepted translations rises from 13 to 43 out of 272; with the tools attached it rises to 55. The gain comes from the bilingual dictionary. For Udmurt, whose dictionary has no English side, the prompt-based condition brings no gain at all, while for the other three languages an English gloss reaches the prompt for 74 to 80% of the source words. Tool calling is also much harder to get working than prompt injection. Of 31 open-weight models, 14 never call a tool, 11 of them because they cannot produce a usable call, and half of the calls that are made name a language the toolkit does not support. We release the data set, every model output and all tool-call logs.

title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
justification: Architectures and KV replay for depth-recurrent LMs; directly tackles KV cache memory growth in decoding.
hype_justification: KV-cache sharing + recurrent LMs trending; Hochreiter group adds visibility.
abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

title: CLEW: Log-Anchored Backward Tracing for Root-Cause Code Localization
justification: Log-anchored root-cause code localization agent; software engineering not inference.
hype_justification: Agentic debugging niche.
abstract: Failures in industrial software systems may involve multiple components and be difficult to reproduce outside the production environment. Root-cause code localization therefore often relies on issue descriptions and runtime logs. However, log evidence may be noisy or incomplete, and the code reporting a symptom may differ from the code containing the underlying defect. These conditions make it challenging to identify relevant log evidence and determine which functions could have caused the reported failure. To address this gap, we introduce CLEW, an agentic approach that combines rule-based log-to-code anchoring with LLM-guided backward code tracing. CLEW organizes selected observations into diagnostic states, guides source exploration from anchored symptom functions, and returns ranked candidate functions, an affected module, and an explanation comprising a proposed mechanism path and associated log events. For evaluation, we construct LogLoc, a benchmark comprising 192 real-world issue and fault-injection cases. Against three baselines, CLEW records the highest observed Acc@1 (77.3%) and MRR (81.3%) on LogLoc-Issues and matches the leading baselines at 97.6% Acc@1 on LogLoc-Airflow. Averaged over all 192 cases, CLEW's wall-clock time is approximately 73% lower than LocAgent's at a similar average inference cost. No aggregate degradation is observed under the tested perturbations, with modest changes in Acc@1 and MRR across the evaluated seeds and base models. These results suggest that CLEW can combine function-level localization with evidence links and runtime efficiency under the evaluated conditions.

title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
justification: Training-free session-local drafting for speculative decoding with verifier KV cache; directly inference serving.
hype_justification: Speculative decoding is hot; thorough energy/latency study but single author.
abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
justification: Program distillation transferring LLM capability to executable programs; reduces inference time but control-task focused.
hype_justification: System-2-to-System-0 framing is catchy, niche benchmark.
abstract: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
justification: Benchmark compiler for evaluating red-team LLM agents; security eval not inference.
hype_justification: Red-team agent benchmark, security-community interest.
abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

title: Could Mobile AI be Exploited?: Understanding the Exploitations of Trust and Ethics Gap in On-Device Small Language Models
justification: Trust/ethics of on-device SLMs; safety of edge models, not inference optimization.
hype_justification: On-device SLM safety is topical, provocative exploitation framing.
abstract: In this paper, we present a very first study to investigate trust and ethical implications of on-device artificial intelligence (AI), focusing on small language models (SLMs) amenable for personal devices like smartphones. While on-device SLMs promise enhanced privacy, reduced latency, and improved user experience compared to cloud-based services, we posit that they might also introduce significant risks and vulnerabilities compared to their on-server counterparts. As part of our study, we conduct a systematic evaluation of the state-of-the-art on-devices SLMs, compared to their on-server counterparts, using well-established trust and ethics frameworks. Our results illustrate that on-device SLMs are significantly less trustworthy and lacks ethical safeguards, specifically demonstrating more stereotypical, unfair, privacy-breaching and harmful content generation behavior. Further, these risks of on-device SLMs could be exploited through Open Knowledge (OkNow) Attacks, and we demonstrated them using potentially unethical vanilla prompts, to which the on-device SLMs answer with valid responses without any filters and without the need for any jailbreaking or prompt engineering. These responses can be abused for various harmful and unethical scenarios like: societal harm, illegal activities, hate, self-harm, exploitable phishing content, disinformation and many others.

title: Pub-Guard-LLM: Detecting Retracted Biomedical Articles with Reliable Explanations
justification: Detecting retracted biomedical articles with LLMs; application not inference.
hype_justification: Retraction-risk tool with benchmark, moderate interest.
abstract: A growing number of scientific articles are retracted each year. Many of these articles continue to be cited and influence research and clinical decisions, posing serious risks. In this paper, we propose Pub-Guard-LLM, a large language model-based system for assessing retraction risks in biomedical articles. The system predicts retraction risks and provides textual explanations. We introduce an open-source benchmark, PubMed Retraction, containing over 12,000 real-world biomedical articles with metadata and retraction labels. Our results show that Pub-Guard-LLM outperforms various baselines. We further show that adding metadata, such as author, institution, and journal information, improves prediction performance. However, metadata can also introduce bias. We study metadata-related bias in retraction risk predictions using a framework for transparent bias detection. To reduce bias, we explore several methods, including retrieval-augmented generation, counterfactual fine-tuning, debate, and argumentation-based approaches. Our results reveal a trade-off between prediction performance and metadata bias. Pub-Guard-LLM provides a step towards reliable and fair retraction risk assessment for biomedical research.

title: Rectifying Conformity Scores for Better Conditional Coverage
justification: Conformal prediction conformity-score rectification; statistics not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Conformal-prediction niche.
abstract: We present a new method for generating confidence sets within the split conformal prediction framework. Our method performs a trainable transformation of any given conformity score to improve conditional coverage while ensuring exact marginal coverage. The transformation is based on an estimate of the conditional quantile of conformity scores. The resulting method is particularly beneficial for constructing adaptive confidence sets in multi-output problems where standard conformal quantile regression approaches have limited applicability. We develop a theoretical bound that captures the influence of the accuracy of the quantile estimate on the approximate conditional validity, unlike classical bounds for conformal prediction methods that only offer marginal coverage. We experimentally show that our method is highly adaptive to the local data structure and outperforms existing methods in terms of conditional coverage, improving the reliability of statistical inference in various applications.

title: OpenClassGen: A Large-Scale Corpus of Real-World Python Classes for LLM Research
justification: Large corpus of Python classes for code-gen research; dataset not inference.
hype_justification: Large-scale dataset release, code-LLM community interest.
abstract: Existing class-level code generation datasets are either synthetic (ClassEval: 100 classes) or insufficient in scale for modern training needs (RealClassEval: 400 classes), hindering robust evaluation and empirical analysis. We present OpenClassGen, a large-scale corpus of 324,843 Python classes extracted from 2,970 engineered open-source projects. Each entry pairs a human-written class with its corresponding skeleton, which comprises class and method signatures with associated docstrings, and is enriched with 27 static code metrics covering complexity, coupling, cohesion, and inheritance properties. Unlike prior benchmarks that require repository-level context resolution, OpenClassGen provides self-contained class skeletons that serve as complete generation specifications. We demonstrate the corpus's utility by evaluating three LLMs (GPT-o4-mini, Claude-4-Sonnet, Qwen-3-Coder) on a curated, executable subset of 300 classes, enriched with test suites achieving 58% branch coverage. Results show strong semantic similarity (CodeBERTScore-F3: 0.89) but moderate functional correctness (pass rate: 0.33), with substantial variance across models. This variance, along with diverse class characteristics, confirms that OpenClassGen enables meaningful differentiation of LLM capabilities. The dataset supports diverse use cases, including fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, difficulty modelling, and failure mode analysis. The complete dataset and curation scripts are publicly available at https://zenodo.org/records/18409150.

title: LiteLMGuard: Seamless and Lightweight On-Device Guardrails for Small Language Models against Quantization Vulnerabilities
justification: On-device guardrails addressing quantization vulnerabilities; touches quantized deployment but about safety filtering.
hype_justification: On-device SLM safety + quantization angle, practical edge interest.
abstract: The growing adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has influenced the development of Small Language Models (SLMs) for on-device deployment across smartphones and edge devices, offering enhanced privacy, reduced latency, server-free functionality, and improved user experience. However, due to on-device resource constraints, SLMs undergo size optimization through compression techniques like quantization, which inadvertently introduce fairness, ethical and privacy risks. Critically, quantized SLMs may respond to harmful queries directly, without requiring adversarial manipulation, raising significant safety and trust concerns. To address this, we propose LiteLMGuard, an on-device guardrail that provides real-time, prompt-level defense for quantized SLMs. Additionally, our guardrail is designed to be model-agnostic such that it can be seamlessly integrated with any SLM, operating independently of underlying architectures. Our LiteLMGuard formalizes deep learning (DL)-based prompt filtering by leveraging semantic understanding to classify prompt answerability for SLMs. Built on our curated Answerable-or-Not dataset, LiteLMGuard employs ELECTRA as the candidate model with 97.75% answerability classification accuracy. The on-device deployment of LiteLMGuard enabled real-time offline filtering with over 85% defense-rate against harmful prompts (including jailbreak attacks), 94% filtering accuracy and ~135 ms average latency. These results demonstrate LiteLMGuard as a lightweight robust defense mechanism for effectively and efficiently securing on-device SLMs against Open Knowledge Attacks.

title: Forests for Differences: Beyond Parametric Difference-in-Differences
justification: Econometric difference-in-differences causal forests; nothing to do with LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche causal-inference methods paper, narrow econometrics audience.
abstract: This paper introduces the Difference-in-Differences Bayesian Causal Forest (DiD-BCF), a novel non-parametric model addressing key challenges in DiD estimation, such as staggered adoption and heterogeneous treatment effects. DiD-BCF provides a unified framework for estimating Average (ATE), Group-Average (GATE), and Conditional Average Treatment Effects (CATE). By structuring separate regression forests for cohort-specific levels, common untreated trends and treatment effects, the model directly embeds conditional parallel trends and no-anticipation restrictions into Bayesian nonparametrics. We establish non-parametric identification and integrated treatment effect consistency of the exact treatment effect posterior distribution. Extensive simulations demonstrate DiD-BCF's superior performance over established benchmarks, particularly under non-linearity, selection biases, and effect heterogeneity. Applied to U.S. minimum wage policy, the model uncovers significant conditional treatment effect heterogeneity related to county population, insights obscured by traditional methods. DiD-BCF offers a robust and versatile tool for more nuanced causal inference in modern DiD applications.

title: BitBypass: A New Direction in Jailbreaking Aligned Large Language Models with Bitstream Camouflage
justification: LLM jailbreak/security attack, not an inference systems paper.
hype_justification: Jailbreak papers get some attention but this is from a small group with narrow novelty.
abstract: The inherent risk of generating harmful and unsafe content by Large Language Models (LLMs), has highlighted the need for their safety alignment. Various techniques like supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning from human feedback, and red-teaming were developed for ensuring the safety alignment of LLMs. However, the robustness of these aligned LLMs is always challenged by adversarial attacks that exploit unexplored and underlying vulnerabilities of the safety alignment. In this paper, we develop a novel black-box jailbreak attack, called BitBypass, that leverages hyphen-separated bitstream camouflage for jailbreaking aligned LLMs. This represents a new direction in jailbreaking by exploiting fundamental information representation of data as continuous bits, rather than leveraging prompt engineering or adversarial manipulations. Our evaluation of five state-of-the-art LLMs, namely GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5, Claude 3.5, Llama 3.1, and Mixtral, in adversarial perspective, revealed the capabilities of BitBypass in bypassing their safety alignment and tricking them into generating harmful and unsafe content. Further, we observed that BitBypass outperforms several state-of-the-art jailbreak attacks in terms of stealthiness and attack success. Overall, these results highlights the effectiveness and efficiency of BitBypass in jailbreaking these state-of-the-art LLMs.

title: Fair Contracts in Principal-Agent Games with Heterogeneous Types
justification: Principal-agent game-theory fairness; unrelated to inference systems.
hype_justification: Theoretical multi-agent fairness, niche venue appeal.
abstract: Fairness is desirable yet challenging to achieve within multi-agent systems, especially when agents differ in latent traits that affect their abilities. This hidden heterogeneity often leads to unequal distributions of wealth, even when agents operate under the same rules. Motivated by real-world examples, we propose a framework based on repeated principal-agent games, where a principal, who also can be seen as a player of the game, learns to offer adaptive contracts to agents. By leveraging a simple yet powerful contract structure, we show that a fairness-aware principal can learn homogeneous linear contracts that equalize outcomes across agents in a sequential social dilemma. Importantly, this fairness does not come at the cost of efficiency: our results demonstrate that it is possible to promote equity and stability in the system while preserving overall performance.

title: Are Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) Suitable for Imbalanced Data Classification?
justification: KANs for imbalanced tabular classification; not about inference systems.
hype_justification: Incremental KAN evaluation, limited broad interest.
abstract: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) parameterize each connection as a learnable univariate B-spline, offering native feature-level interpretability. Whether this locality helps or hinders under class imbalance, where minority sparsity may leave spline edges without enough local observations to update reliably, remains unexamined. We evaluate KANs against capacity-matched Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) and XGBoost across ten imbalanced tabular datasets under three conditions: native class distribution, Focal Loss, and SMOTE-Tomek resampling, within a parameter-parity, two-phase framework. Under the native distribution, KAN spline activations collapse in minority-sparse regions, showing stronger majority-class bias than the matched MLP. Focal Loss yields negligible improvement, as it reweights gradients without providing the localized observations needed for discriminative curvature. Conversely, SMOTE-Tomek resampling lets spline activations recover structured minority-class representations, achieving the best cohort-wide rank and a large, statistically significant gain over unmitigated KANs, though not over resampled baselines. KAN's native spline interpretability directly reveals these dynamics via learned activation profiles, proving representational change rather than threshold recalibration without post-hoc attribution. However, these interpretability gains incur substantially higher training overhead than a parameter-matched MLP across all conditions, with no strategy-dependent latency reduction. Thus, KANs are conditionally suitable for imbalanced tabular classification: effective and interpretable with data-level resampling, yet costly relative to simpler alternatives without it.

title: A Survey on Cloud-Edge-Terminal Collaborative Intelligence in AIoT Networks
justification: Cloud-edge-terminal AIoT survey touches LLM deployment but not inference systems specifically.
hype_justification: Broad tutorial survey, moderate reference value but not a hot method.
abstract: The proliferation of Internet of things (IoT) devices in smart cities, transportation, healthcare, and industrial applications, coupled with the explosive growth of AI-driven services, has increased demands for efficient distributed computing architectures and networks, driving cloud-edge-terminal collaborative intelligence (CETCI) as a fundamental paradigm within the artificial intelligence of things (AIoT) community. With advancements in deep learning, large language models (LLMs), and edge computing, CETCI has made significant progress with emerging AIoT applications, moving beyond isolated layer optimization to deployable collaborative intelligence systems for AIoT (CISAIOT), a practical research focus in AI, distributed computing, and communications. This survey describes foundational architectures, enabling technologies, and scenarios of CETCI paradigms, offering a tutorial-style review for CISAIOT beginners. We systematically analyze architectural components spanning cloud, edge, and terminal layers, examining core technologies including network virtualization, container orchestration, and software-defined networking, while presenting categorizations of collaboration paradigms that cover task offloading, resource allocation, and optimization across heterogeneous infrastructures. Furthermore, we explain intelligent collaboration learning frameworks by reviewing advances in federated learning, distributed deep learning, edge-cloud model evolution, and reinforcement learning-based methods. Finally, we discuss challenges (e.g., scalability, heterogeneity, interoperability) and future trends (e.g., 6G+, agents, quantum computing, digital twin), highlighting how integration of distributed computing and communication can address open issues and guide development of robust, efficient, and secure collaborative AIoT systems.

title: UncertainGen: Scalable Uncertainty-Aware Representation Learning of DNA Sequences
justification: DNA sequence representation learning; genomics, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche bioinformatics method.
abstract: Learning effective representations of DNA sequences is fundamental to genomic data analysis, especially in the presence of high sequence similarity and inter-species DNA sharing. Existing approaches rely on deterministic embeddings, such as k-mer statistics or representations from large language models, which fail to capture the inherent uncertainty in short and ambiguous DNA fragments. We propose UncertainGen, a lightweight probabilistic representation learning framework that embeds DNA sequences as distributions in a latent space. The learned embedding variance captures positional ambiguity, increasing for sequences compatible with multiple genomic clusters. We establish theoretical guarantees on embedding distinguishability, and show that the probabilistic formulation induces a data-adaptive metric that expands the effective representational space. We evaluate UncertainGen in the metagenomic binning task to demonstrate the practical benefits of uncertainty-aware representations. Experiments show that probabilistic embeddings consistently outperform deterministic k-mer and large genome foundation models, while remaining lightweight and efficient.

title: Test-Time Search in Neural Graph Coarsening Procedures for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem
justification: Neural graph coarsening for vehicle routing; combinatorial optimization, not inference.
hype_justification: Narrow OR/ML topic.
abstract: The identification of valid inequalities, such as the rounded capacity inequalities (RCIs), is a key component of cutting plane methods for the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP). While a deep learning-based separation method can learn to find high-quality cuts, our analysis reveals that the model produces fewer cuts than expected because it is insufficiently sensitive to generate a diverse set of generated subsets. This paper proposes an alternative: enhancing the performance of a trained model at inference time through a new test-time search with stochasticity. First, we introduce stochastic edge selection into the graph coarsening procedure, replacing the previously proposed greedy approach. Second, we propose the Graph Coarsening History-based Partitioning (GraphCHiP) algorithm, which leverages coarsening history to identify not only RCIs but also, for the first time, the Framed capacity inequalities (FCIs). Experiments on randomly generated CVRP instances demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in reducing the dual gap compared to the existing neural separation method. Additionally, our method discovers effective FCIs on a specific instance, despite the challenging nature of identifying such cuts.

title: Prediction-Augmented Trees for Reliable Statistical Inference
justification: Statistical inference with prediction-augmented trees; 'inference' is statistical, not LLM serving.
hype_justification: Solid stats method, limited LLM-community attention.
abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly central to scientific discovery, but translating ML predictions into rigorous scientific claims still requires statistical inference on gold-standard labeled data. A setting that has emerged across the sciences provides the analyst with a small labeled sample, a much larger unlabeled sample, and a pre-trained predictor, with the goal of constructing a confidence interval for a quantity of interest, as was formalized in Angelopoulos et al. (2023). In this ML-driven scientific discovery literature, labeled data is typically the binding constraint on precision while computation is comparatively unconstrained, motivating the design question of how additional computation can extract more inferential value from a fixed labeled set, a fixed unlabeled set, and a fixed predictor. To address this question, we propose the Prediction-Augmented Residual Tree (PART) estimator. PART takes the same inputs as the original PPI estimator and replaces its single global rectifier with locally computed rectifiers obtained from an adaptive partition of the feature space. We show that PART outperforms existing methods by producing tighter confidence intervals across real-world datasets from ecology, astronomy, and census reports, among other domains. We then describe and analyze PAQ, an estimator based on numerical quadrature techniques. Under appropriate assumptions on the input data, we show that the variance of PAQ shrinks at a rate of $O(N^{-1} + n^{-4})$, showing that there are settings where the rate of $O(N^{-1}+n^{-1})$ of existing methods can be provably broken.

title: Beyond Synthetic Benchmarks: Evaluating LLM Performance on Real-World Class-Level Code Generation
justification: Class-level code generation benchmark; LLM capability eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Code-gen benchmarks are popular but this is incremental from a less prominent group.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly from well-studied function-level code generation to emerging repository-level approaches, yet this progression reveals a critical gap: class-level code generation, which is the fundamental building block connecting individual functions to complete repositories, remains systematically underexplored. Understanding class-level capabilities is a prerequisite to repository-level success, as current approaches cannot distinguish whether failures stem from basic implementation deficiencies or sophisticated context management issues. We introduce RealClassEval, a benchmark derived from real-world open-source repositories, comprising 400 classes divided into seen and unseen partitions based on model training cutoffs. Our systematic evaluation across seven state-of-the-art LLMs reveals fundamental limitations masked by synthetic benchmarks: while LLMs achieve 84 to 89% correctness on synthetic tasks, they attain only 25 to 34% on real-world classes, with minimal distinction between seen and unseen codebases. Notably, this performance range converges with concurrent work using rich natural language descriptions and repository context, suggesting that specification complexity cannot overcome core implementation bottlenecks. Documentation provides marginal improvements (1 to 3%), while retrieval augmentation yields greater gains (4 to7%), specifically with incomplete specifications. Error analysis reveals AttributeError, TypeError, and AssertionError dominate 84% of failures, with distinct patterns between synthetic (logic-focused) and real-world (object-oriented) scenarios. These findings establish the diagnostic foundation necessary for advancing both fundamental LLM capabilities and sophisticated repository-level approaches, while providing actionable guidance for production deployment strategies.

title: Re(Visiting) Time Series Foundation Models in Finance
justification: Time series foundation models for finance; application, not inference optimization.
hype_justification: Cautionary empirical finance study, modest reach.
abstract: Financial time series forecasting is vital for trading, portfolio optimization, and risk management but is challenged by noisy, nonstationary, and heterogeneous data. Time series foundation models (TSFMs), inspired by large language models, aim to learn transferable temporal representations. Whether pre-training on massive, diverse datasets enables similar generalization to finance remains an open question. This study provides a comprehensive empirical evaluation of TSFMs in global financial markets using large-scale daily excess-return data. We assess zero-shot inference, fine-tuning, and pre-training from scratch against strong benchmarks. Off-the-shelf TSFMs generally perform poorly, while finance-native pre-training improves long-window gross portfolio performance. Larger pre-training datasets and synthetic augmentation improve selected specifications, particularly at longer input windows. Configuration changes have mixed effects across forecasting and portfolio metrics, and TSFMs do not consistently outperform strong benchmarks. These findings caution against uncritical AI adoption in finance, where insufficient validation can lead to unreliable forecasts and substantial financial losses.

title: VeruSAGE-Bench: A Benchmark Suite for Rust System Verification
justification: Rust system verification benchmark for LLMs; capability eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Microsoft Research authors and a hot formal-verification/agent theme may draw interest.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown impressive capability to understand and develop code. However, their capability to rigorously reason about and formally prove the correctness of software systems remains in question. Current benchmarks for formal proof generation focus on isolated tasks, typically algorithmic-style problems utilizing basic data structures. We curate a new benchmark suite for system-level proof generation, VeruSAGE-Bench, which consists of 849 proof tasks extracted from eight open-source Verus-verified Rust systems, covering operating systems, storage systems, memory allocators, and more. These tasks are much more complicated than those in previous benchmarks, containing on average more than 20x the formal specification (in Lines of Code) and requiring a much broader array of verification techniques. We evaluate six LLMs on VeruSAGE-Bench (o4-mini, GPT-5, Sonnet 4, Sonnet 4.5, Opus 4.5, Qwen3.5), and demonstrate that different models and agentic setups lead to vastly different success rates and costs. We also show that the best models possess impressive capability in writing correctness proofs and hence should inspire new ways of developing trustworthy software. Meanwhile, some difficult tasks in VeruSAGE-Bench stress even the best model, forcing long reasoning time (over an hour on the hardest tasks, 15.3 min per task on average), high token cost (USD 13.65 per task on average), and proof failures, which we hope will guide future improvements in models and agents. This is particularly true for a harder no-lemma version of VeruSAGE-Bench, where the helper lemmas written by human experts are removed: there, the best model proves only 41% of the tasks from the hardest project, at USD 96 per task.

title: Exploring the Potential of Spiking Neural Networks in UWB NLOS Identification
justification: Spiking NN for UWB NLOS; edge efficiency but not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Narrow neuromorphic/localization letter.
abstract: Ultrawideband (UWB) nonline-of-sight (NLOS) identification is critical for accurate localization, yet prevailing deep learning solutions impose computational demands incompatible with low-cost edge devices. This letter explores the potential of spiking neural networks (SNNs) for this task and develops a fully unsupervised SNN solution. Against supervised deep learning baselines, our approach achieves comparable accuracy (~82%) with only 4.7K synaptic operations (SOPs) per inference, representing a three-order-of-magnitude improvement in efficiency. These results establish that SNNs can serve as a viable neuromorphic alternative for edge UWB applications.

title: CD4LM: Consistency Distillation and aDaptive Decoding for Diffusion Language Models
justification: Consistency distillation + adaptive decoding to accelerate diffusion language model inference, 9.7x speedup.
hype_justification: AMD authors (Barsoum, Z. Liu), diffusion-LM acceleration is trending, code released.
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) accelerate generation by decoding multiple tokens in parallel, but pushing them to fast decoding often sacrifices accuracy. We attribute this to a static-to-dynamic mismatch: training optimizes local denoising under fixed schedules, while fast inference skips steps and encounters irregular mask patterns. Existing accelerators largely address only one side of this problem. Training-free inference methods speed up decoding without changing the model, leaving the mismatch unresolved; training-side distillation methods adapt the model, but often tie the student to a specific decoding trajectory, limiting composability and still suffering accuracy loss. We propose CD4LM, a composable framework for accurate DLM acceleration. Its core training component, Discrete-Space Consistency Distillation (DSCD) trains a trajectory-invariant student on diverse masked states, reducing the mismatch without fixing a decoding policy. We pair DSCD with a lightweight ConfidenceAdaptive Decoder, while keeping the trained student compatible with external inference-side accelerators. On GSM8K, CD4LM preserves accuracy while achieving a 5.18x speedup; stacking CD4LM with per-step cache accelerators further pushes speedup to 9.73x at teacher-level accuracy, suggesting a scalable path for combining training-side robustness with future decoding advances. Code is available at https://github.com/yihao-liang/CDLM.

title: MHRC-Bench: A Multilingual Hardware Repository-Level Code Completion benchmark
justification: Multilingual hardware (HDL) code completion benchmark; LLM eval, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Niche hardware code-completion benchmark.
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance on code completion in general-purpose programming languages, but existing repository-level benchmarks focus almost exclusively on software code and largely overlook hardware description languages (HDLs). We present \textbf{MHRC-Bench}, consisting of \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Train} and \textbf{MHRC-Bench-Eval}, the first benchmark for multilingual hardware code completion at the repository level with functional evaluation. MHRC-Bench covers three major hardware design coding styles and annotates each completion target with code-structure-level and hardware-oriented semantic labels derived from concrete syntax tree (CST) analysis. Post-training billion-scale code LLMs on MHRC-Bench-Train enables smaller open-weight models to outperform much larger general-purpose models under matched context windows. Beyond aggregate accuracy, our analysis surfaces four findings that distinguish hardware from software code completion: \emph{(i)}~performance varies sharply across HDLs, with high-level synthesis (HLS) easiest and VHDL hardest in most settings across functional pass rate, exact match (EM), and edit similarity (ES); \emph{(ii)}~hardware accuracy is non-monotonic in code-structure depth, in contrast with the monotonic depth--accuracy curve known for software; \emph{(iii)}~accuracy plateaus once the input context exceeds 2{,}048 tokens, while software completion continues to benefit from longer context; and \emph{(iv)}~certain repository-level retrievers tuned on software underperform a no-retrieval baseline on HDL repositories because their structural and dependency assumptions are violated by hardware code.

title: Advancing ESG Intelligence: An Expert-level Agent and Comprehensive Benchmark for Sustainable Finance
justification: ESG multi-agent analysis system; vertical application, not inference.
hype_justification: Domain agent/benchmark, limited broad appeal.
abstract: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria are essential for evaluating corporate sustainability and ethical performance. However, professional ESG analysis is hindered by data fragmentation across unstructured sources, and existing large language models (LLMs) often struggle with the complex, multi-step workflows required for rigorous auditing. To address these limitations, we introduce ESGAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system empowered by a specialized toolset, including retrieval augmentation, web search and domain-specific functions, to generate in-depth ESG analysis. Complementing this agentic system, we present a comprehensive three-level benchmark derived from 310 corporate sustainability reports, designed to evaluate capabilities ranging from atomic common-sense questions to the generation of integrated, in-depth analysis. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that ESGAgent outperforms state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs with an average accuracy of 84.15% on atomic question-answering tasks, and excels in professional report generation by integrating rich charts and verifiable references. These findings confirm the diagnostic value of our benchmark, establishing it as a vital testbed for assessing general and advanced agentic capabilities in high-stakes vertical domains.

title: VIOLA: Towards Video In-Context Learning with Minimal Annotations
justification: Video in-context learning with minimal annotation; MLLM adaptation, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Label-efficient MLLM work, moderate niche interest.
abstract: Generalizing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to novel video domains is essential for real-world deployment but remains challenging due to the scarcity of labeled data. While In-Context Learning (ICL) offers a training-free adaptation path, standard methods rely on large annotated pools, which are often impractical in specialized environments like industrial or surgical settings since they require the experts' annotations. To bridge this gap, we introduce VIOLA (Video In-cOntext Learning with minimal Annotation), a label-efficient framework that synergizes minimal expert supervision with abundant unlabeled data. First, to maximize the efficiency of a strict annotation budget, we propose density-uncertainty-weighted sampling. Unlike standard diversity or uncertainty strategies that risk selecting visual outliers, our method leverages density estimation to identify samples that are simultaneously diverse, representative, and informative. Second, to utilize the remaining unlabeled data without noise propagation, we construct a hybrid pool and introduce confidence-aware retrieval and confidence-aware prompting. These mechanisms explicitly model label reliability, retrieving demonstrations based on a composite score of similarity and confidence while enabling the MLLM to adaptively distinguish between verified ground truths and noisy pseudo-labels. Extensive experiments across nine diverse benchmarks using three MLLMs demonstrate that our framework significantly outperforms various baselines in low-resource settings, achieving robust adaptation with minimal annotation costs. Project page: https://fujiry0.github.io/VIOLA-project-page/

title: WAXAL: A Large-Scale Multilingual African Language Speech Corpus
justification: African-language speech corpus; dataset for ASR/TTS, not inference systems.
hype_justification: Google-released large multilingual dataset likely gets dataset attention.
abstract: Recent advances in speech technology predominantly favor high-resource languages, leaving speakers of Sub-Saharan African languages underserved. To bridge this divide, we introduce WAXAL, an open, large-scale speech dataset spanning 27 African languages representing over 100 million speakers. WAXAL comprises over 14,100 hours of speech collected in partnership with African academic and community organizations to build local research capacity: an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) corpus with 2,340 hours of transcribed, image-prompted natural speech across 19 languages (plus ~11,760 untranscribed hours) and a studio-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) corpus of ~247 hours across 15 language configurations. We empirically benchmark three architecturally distinct ASR models -- Gemma 3n 2B, Whisper-Large-v3, and MMS-1B-all -- across the 19 ASR languages on strictly speaker-disjoint splits. Fine-tuning on WAXAL yields substantial gains, reducing macro-average WER by up to 58% for Whisper-Large-v3, 56% for Gemma 3n 2B, and 17% for MMS-1B-all (and Character Error Rate by up to 70%). WAXAL-fine-tuned models generalize zero-shot to three out-of-distribution benchmarks: FLEURS, Mozilla Common Voice, and Sunbird SALT. Finally, an LLM-as-judge semantic evaluation confirms that fine-tuning preserves speaker intent beyond surface-level transcription metrics. WAXAL is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/WaxalNLP.

title: A Comparative Study of UMAP and Other Dimensionality Reduction Methods
justification: UMAP dimensionality-reduction comparison; unrelated.
hype_justification: Incremental comparative stats study.
abstract: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is a widely used manifold learning technique for dimensionality reduction. This paper studies UMAP, supervised UMAP, and several competing dimensionality reduction methods, including Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Kernel PCA, Sliced Inverse Regression (SIR), Kernel SIR, and t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding, through a comprehensive comparative analysis. Although UMAP has attracted substantial attention for preserving local and global structures, its supervised extensions, particularly for regression settings, remain rather underexplored. We provide a systematic evaluation of supervised UMAP for both regression and classification using simulated and real datasets, with performance assessed via predictive accuracy on low-dimensional embeddings. Our results show that supervised UMAP performs well for classification but exhibits limitations in effectively incorporating response information for regression, highlighting an important direction for future development.

title: The Challenge of Out-Of-Distribution Detection in Motor Imagery BCIs
justification: OOD detection in motor-imagery BCIs; EEG, not LLM inference.
hype_justification: Niche BCI benchmark.
abstract: Machine Learning classifiers used in Brain-Computer Interfaces make classifications based on the distribution of examples on which they were trained. When exposed to EEG from unfamiliar classes, they can only make blind guesses. Instead of allowing such guesses, these Out-of-Distribution (OOD) samples should be detected and rejected to improve the robustness of BCIs against unfamiliar cognitive states. We study OOD detection in Motor Imagery BCIs by training a model on some classes and observing whether an unfamiliar movement class can be detected based on increased uncertainty. We tested seven different OOD detection methods and one more method that has been claimed to boost the quality of OOD detection. For many BCI users, the uncertainty for the familiar in-distribution classes can still be higher than for the out-of-distribution classes, due to the high intrinsic variability inherent in EEG signals. As a result, many OOD detection methods that have shown good performance in other machine learning domains prove to be ineffective at identifying unfamiliar motor imagery patterns in BCIs. However, we also found that OOD detection performance is correlated with on-task performance, and that Deep Ensemble models and MC-Dropout models were able to achieve on-task AUROC > 0.9, and OOD detection ability up to 0.7. This shows that for models and subjects where task performance is high, rejecting unfamiliar cognitive states becomes feasible. Our research demonstrates a Leave-One-Class-Out OOD detection setup as an experimental paradigm for studying whether models are robust against unfamiliar motor imagery actions that were not seen in the training data. This is the first benchmark in Motor Imagery BCI that evaluates this type of OOD data. Our results demonstrate how to improve the overall safety and reliability of BCIs by preventing erroneous actions.

title: Is Agentic AI Ready for Real-World Hardware Engineering? A Deep Dive with Phoenix-bench
